title: Cost as a design constraint
summary: Cost is a design constraint like latency or availability: every architectural choice has a price, and the right design meets the requirement at the lowest sustainable spend. This lesson lays out what a cloud bill is made of and which transfers are free, unit economics as the measure that makes spend comparable, the design levers that change the bill with the discounts each carries, the FinOps operating model, the cost of each extra nine, what a design document's cost section must contain, and a worked costing of one pipeline two ways from dated unit prices.

blocks.text: The same post is candid about what the comparison leaves out: a company entirely in the cloud with no racks would pay for colocation too, the savings estimate excludes some of those costs, and the lead time for new servers is weeks rather than minutes. The team running the systems stayed the same size through the move, which is the claim the post rests on for the operating cost.

Google's SRE book records how Bigtable's cost was made visible to its users: low-latency clusters with slack capacity for services that need them, and throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy at perhaps 10 to 50 percent of the cost, so that each client picks the level of service with the lowest cost that still meets its needs. The chapter presents the same logic for products, with an availability target that is exceeded but not by much, because the margin would otherwise be spent on features or technical debt.

AWS's own cost pillar gives its consumption-model example with numbers: development and test environments are typically used for eight hours a day during the working week, and stopping them when not in use is a potential saving of 75 percent, 40 hours against 168. The Lambda pricing page's worked example applies a 72 percent three-year Compute Savings Plan discount to an on-demand instance price, which is the rate lever stated by the provider rather than estimated.

subtopics.title: What the bill is made of

blocks.text: A cloud bill is a sum of metered units, and a designer who knows the units can read a design as a bill. Compute is sold by instance hour or, for serverless functions, by request and by memory-seconds; storage by gigabyte-month per class, with requests and retrievals charged separately; managed services by request, by throughput unit or by provisioned capacity; and the network by the gigabyte for the paths that are not free. AWS's own pricing pages give the shape: a function costs a fee per million requests plus a fee per gigabyte-second of duration, an object store charges a small fee per thousand GET requests on top of storage, and an instance has an hourly on-demand price that commitment discounts reduce.

blocks.text: Data transfer is the term designers forget, and the AWS architecture blog on the subject sets out the rules. Inbound transfer from the internet is free across services and regions; transfer within one Availability Zone is free; transfer out to the internet is charged per service at the originating region's rates; reaching public service endpoints through an internet gateway in the same region carries no transfer charge, but the same path through a NAT gateway carries a data processing charge; and Transit Gateway adds an hourly charge per attachment plus processing per gigabyte.

The consequence for a design is that the cheapest topology keeps chatty components in one zone where latency allows, places replicas across zones deliberately rather than by accident, and routes traffic to managed services through endpoints rather than NAT. The line that surprises most teams is cross-zone chatter between tiers that were spread across zones for availability without anyone pricing the replication and the calls between them.

Write the design as a list of metered units before pricing it: instance hours, requests, gigabyte-seconds, gigabyte-months per class, gigabytes out by destination. If a unit cannot be named, the cost cannot be estimated.

subtopics.title: Unit economics: cost per unit of value

blocks.text: Total spend says little on its own. The FinOps principles state that unit economic and value-based metrics demonstrate business impact better than aggregate or categorised spend, and that business value, not cost alone, drives technology decisions: conscious trade-offs among cost, quality and speed. The unit is whatever the product sells or serves: a request, an active user, a tenant, a gigabyte stored, a job processed. Spend divided by that unit is the number that stays comparable as the product grows.

Azure's first cost principle is to develop a cost model before any tracking: a model that segments expenses, estimates total cost of ownership including support and implementation, identifies the cost drivers early and predicts how growth or shrinkage changes spending. Google's first principle is the same from the other side: cloud resources must deliver measurable business value, which requires aligning spending with business objectives, and a culture in which everyone considering a change has the cost information to weigh it.

blocks.title: From a monthly bill to a unit cost
items: Take one month's bill for the service, tagged to it: $18,000 (assumption).
Count the units served in the month: 60 million requests (assumption).
Unit cost: $18,000 divided by 60 million is $0.0003 per request, or $0.30 per 1,000 requests.
Find the dominant term: egress at $7,200 is 40 percent of the bill, so it is the term the design should attack first.
Compare over time: the month before was $0.33 per 1,000 requests, so the unit cost fell while the bill rose, which is healthy growth.
Set the budget line as a unit cost, $0.30 per 1,000 requests, and alert on it, not on the total.

blocks.text: Two unit costs are usually needed: a resource efficiency metric, such as cost per million requests, which engineers can act on, and a business metric, such as cost per active customer, which product and finance can act on, with the relation between them documented. A design that cannot be expressed in both has either a missing tag or a missing definition of what it is for.
Report spend as a unit cost against the unit the product sells. Total spend rising while unit cost falls is growth; the reverse is a design problem, whatever the total.

subtopics.title: The levers that change the bill

blocks.text: The AWS cost pillar's principles name the levers in order. Adopt a consumption model: pay only for what is consumed and scale usage with the business; its example is a development environment used eight hours a day on working days, which can be stopped outside those hours for a potential saving of 75 percent, 40 hours against 168. Measure overall efficiency as business output against cost. Stop spending on undifferentiated heavy lifting by using managed services where they remove operational work. Analyse and attribute expenditure so that owners see their own costs.

The pillar's demand-and-supply guidance adds the two mechanisms behind the consumption model. Supply can be matched to demand just in time, eliminating overprovisioning, but balanced against the need to provision for resource failures, high availability and provisioning time. And demand itself can be modified with a throttle, a buffer or a queue to smooth it and serve it with fewer resources, provided the acceptable and maximum delay of the workload is known.

blocks.text: The levers interact with the other constraints. Commitments reduce the rate but not the usage, so right-size first and commit second. Spot and scale-to-zero cut cost by accepting interruption or startup delay, which the reliability and capacity lessons price in minutes of error budget and seconds of startup. Per-request pricing is the cheapest design at low volume and the most expensive at high volume, so the choice must be rechecked as load grows, with the crossover computed from the unit prices rather than assumed.
Usage first, then rate: remove waste and match supply to demand before buying commitments, and recheck serverless against a fleet at each doubling of load.

FinOps, in the FinOps Foundation's definition, is an operational framework and cultural practice that maximises the business value of technology, enables timely data-driven decisions, and creates financial accountability through collaboration between engineering, finance and business teams. It is performed by working iteratively through three phases. In Inform, the organisation examines cost, usage and efficiency data: ingestion, allocation, reporting, forecasting and unit economics. In Optimize, it identifies opportunities such as rightsizing, modern architectures and the elimination of waste. In Operate, it builds the policies, automation and cadence that keep the first two going, and the page is explicit that the phases are cycled rapidly rather than completed once.

blocks.text: Allocation is what makes ownership real: every resource carries the tags or labels that map it to a team, a service and an environment, shared platform costs are split by a stated rule, and the result is shown back to each team as its own spend and unit cost. Azure's principle of cost-management discipline adds the governance: an accountability model with assigned roles, realistic budgets covering functional and non-functional requirements and growth, notifications when thresholds are exceeded, and a channel for communicating the cost implications of design changes learned from production.

The AWS pillar frames the same culture as cloud financial management, a capability to be built deliberately with knowledge, programmes and processes, in the same way an organisation builds security or operations capability, and it asks for expenditure to be analysed and attributed so that usage changes where the owners are.
Tag at creation through the infrastructure code, show each team its spend and unit cost, and put a budget with an alert on every service. A cost nobody owns is a cost nobody reduces.

subtopics.title: Trading cost against reliability and performance

blocks.text: The SRE book's chapter on risk states the shape of the reliability cost curve: cost does not rise linearly with reliability, and an incremental improvement may cost a hundred times the previous one, in redundant compute and equipment and in the opportunity cost of engineers not building features. Users mostly cannot tell: a user on a smartphone that is 99 percent reliable cannot distinguish a service at four nines from one at five. So the target is set where the business value of the extra reliability exceeds its cost, and then treated as both a minimum and a maximum.

blocks.caption: The chapter's worked trade-off for one more nine, where every request has equal value.
rows: $900: the most the extra nine may cost before it loses money

blocks.text: The chapter's infrastructure example is the pattern for a design: Bigtable offers low-latency clusters with slack capacity and more redundancy for clients that need them, and throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy for clients that do not, the latter at perhaps 10 to 50 percent of the cost. Delineated levels of service expose the cost difference to clients, who then pick the cheapest level that meets their need: critical data in the globally consistent store, optional data in the cheaper eventually consistent one.

Azure's principles say the same about every quality: expect trade-offs with security, scalability, resilience and operability, and make them against stated requirements rather than by default. In a design that means a target per component, not per system: a checkout path may justify multi-zone active redundancy while a reporting job runs on interruptible capacity and retries, and a stated latency or retention requirement is priced before it is granted.

Price each quality per component: the cost of single-zone, multi-zone and multi-region for this tier, against the revenue or budget the extra protection defends. Pick the cheapest option that meets the stated target.

A design document carries a cost section the way it carries a capacity section, and the two share their inputs. The section states the metered units the design consumes, the unit prices with their date and source, the monthly cost at the planned load and at ten times it, the dominant term, the unit cost against the product's unit, and at least one alternative at a different cost point with its consequences. Google's pillar asks for the review to continue after launch, optimising continuously and addressing inefficiencies before they become significant; Azure's asks that cost implications learned from production feed back into design.

blocks.text: The most useful line in the section is the crossover: the load at which the chosen option stops being the cheapest, computed from the unit prices. A serverless pipeline that is cheapest at a million events a day may cost more than a small fleet at a hundred million, and a design that states the crossover gives the team a trigger for the migration rather than a surprise on the bill.
No design review without a cost table: units, dated prices, the dominant term at planned load and at 10x, the unit cost, and the alternative. A paragraph of estimates hides the term that matters.

worked_example.title: Worked example: costing a thumbnail pipeline two ways

blocks.text: A photo product generates thumbnails for every upload and serves them to the web. The team costs the pipeline on serverless functions and on a small instance fleet. Prices marked stated are taken from the AWS pricing pages as of 2026-10-15 and cited; prices marked assumed are stand-ins that must be checked against the price list before the number is used. The script after the steps recomputes everything.

blocks.title: From uploads to a monthly bill and a unit cost
items: Uploads: 50 million a month (assumption), each producing one function invocation.
Function duration: 1 GB of memory for 0.5 seconds per image (assumption, from a test), so 25 million GB-seconds a month.
Function duration cost: 25 million times $0.0000167 per GB-second (stated) is about $418.
Function requests: 50 million at $0.20 per million (stated) is $10.
Thumbnail reads: 200 million GET requests a month (assumption) at $0.0004 per 1,000 (stated) is $80.
Storage growth: 50 million thumbnails of 200 kB is 10 TB a month, at an assumed $0.023 per GB-month, about $230 for the first month and growing by that each month.
Egress: 200 million reads of 200 kB is 40 TB a month to the internet, at an assumed $0.09 per GB, about $3,600.
Serverless total in month one: about $4,340, of which egress is 83 percent, so egress is the dominant term, not compute.
Fleet alternative: 3 m7g.xlarge instances (assumption) at $0.1632 per hour on demand (stated) for 730 hours is about $357 a month, idle at night.
Fleet with commitment: the 72 percent three-year Compute Savings Plan discount in the Lambda page's example gives about $100 a month, but commits for three years.
Crossover: compute is $428 serverless against $357 on demand at 50 million uploads, so the fleet wins only slightly here and loses at lower volume; the choice is not where the money is.
The lever: a CDN in front of the thumbnails at an assumed 90 percent hit rate cuts origin egress to 4 TB, about $360, if the CDN's own per-gigabyte price is lower, which must be checked on its page.
Unit cost: about $4,340 over 50 million uploads is $0.087 per 1,000 uploads before the CDN, and about $1,100 over 50 million, $0.022 per 1,000, after it.
The decider: egress. The compute choice moves tens of dollars; the delivery path moves thousands, and the design review should spend its time there.

blocks.caption: The cost section as the review should receive it: month one at 50 million uploads.
rows: stated on the S3 page's example
assumed; charged per service and region
stated on the Lambda page's example

blocks.code:
# unit prices as of 2026-10-15; 'stated' ones are on the cited pricing pages, 'assumed' ones must be checked
uploads = 50_000_000
reads = 200_000_000
thumb_bytes = 200_000
gb_seconds_per_image = 1.0 * 0.5

price_gb_second = 0.0000167     # stated
price_per_m_requests = 0.20     # stated
price_get_per_1000 = 0.0004     # stated
price_storage_gb_month = 0.023  # assumed
price_egress_gb = 0.09          # assumed
price_instance_hour = 0.1632    # stated, m7g.xlarge on demand

compute = uploads * gb_seconds_per_image * price_gb_second + uploads / 1e6 * price_per_m_requests
gets = reads / 1000 * price_get_per_1000
storage = uploads * thumb_bytes / 1e9 * price_storage_gb_month
egress = reads * thumb_bytes / 1e9 * price_egress_gb
fleet = 3 * 730 * price_instance_hour

total = compute + gets + storage + egress
print(f"serverless compute {compute:,.0f}  gets {gets:,.0f}  storage {storage:,.0f}  egress {egress:,.0f}  total {total:,.0f}")
print(f"fleet on demand {fleet:,.0f}; egress share {egress / total:.0%}; unit cost {total / uploads * 1000:.3f} per 1,000 uploads")
